source.title: Menstrual Cycle Phase–Based Strength & Conditioning Training for Elite Team Sport Female Athletes

paper.citation: Moore S.R., Bruinvels G., Smith-Ryan A.E. Menstrual Cycle Phase–Based Strength & Conditioning Training for Elite Team Sport Female Athletes. Strength & Conditioning Journal. 2024. doi:10.1519/SSC.0000000000000879.
paper.abstract: This paper addresses the following question: How might practitioners organize menstrual-cycle-informed strength and conditioning for eumenorrheic elite team-sport athletes while accounting for physiology, individual variation, privacy, and total stress? Participants: No intervention cohort; the proposed model targets eumenorrheic elite female team-sport athletes. Sport and level: Collegiate and professional team sport. Design: Evidence- and experience-based applied narrative. Exposure or intervention: Proposed adjustment of training stress across menstrual-cycle phases.
paper.tldr: The authors state that performance changes across the menstrual cycle appear highly individual, so their model is not based on a universal acute-performance response. The proposed periodization model targets a theorized capacity for adaptation while balancing training stress and recovery, rather than using symptoms or cycle phase alone. Begin with voluntary education, informed consent, secure data handling, and athlete-specific observations.
paper.methods: Design: Evidence- and experience-based applied narrative. Exposure or intervention: Proposed adjustment of training stress across menstrual-cycle phases. Comparator: None. Measurements and outcomes: Theoretical adaptive capacity, symptoms, performance, recovery, health, and athlete experience. Analysis: Physiological rationale, practical model construction, privacy considerations, and future research directions.
paper.findings: The authors state that performance changes across the menstrual cycle appear highly individual, so their model is not based on a universal acute-performance response. The proposed periodization model targets a theorized capacity for adaptation while balancing training stress and recovery, rather than using symptoms or cycle phase alone. The authors identify the absence of an evidence-based team-sport resource for cycle-based strength-and-conditioning periodization as the gap their applied model seeks to address.
paper.limitations: This is a proposed applied model, not evidence that phase-based programming improves performance, health, or injury outcomes. The authors explicitly acknowledge individual performance variation and emphasize privacy considerations. Interpretation: Calendar-based assumptions should not override the athlete's measured response, preferences, hormonal context, or right not to disclose sensitive health data.
paper.practicalImplications: Begin with voluntary education, informed consent, secure data handling, and athlete-specific observations. If cycle information is used, treat it as contextual data alongside symptoms, readiness, schedule, and training history. Avoid mandatory phase rules or reduced expectations based solely on cycle timing; the present paper is a hypothesis-generating programming framework.
